flashcards.back_definition: An IDS watches a copy of the traffic and alerts. An IPS sits inline and can block malicious traffic as it happens.
flashcards.back_example: An IPS drops a packet matching a known exploit before it reaches the server.
flashcards.back_confusion: A badly tuned IPS with many false positives blocks legitimate traffic and causes outages.

flashcards.back_definition: Signature-based matches known attack patterns: precise but blind to new attacks. Anomaly-based flags departures from a learned normal: catches novel attacks but raises more false positives.
flashcards.back_example: A signature catches a known exploit string; anomaly detection catches a printer suddenly uploading gigabytes.
flashcards.back_hook: Signature knows the face; anomaly notices odd behaviour.

flashcards.front: True positive, false positive, true negative, false negative?
flashcards.back_definition: TP: real attack, alert raised. FP: benign activity, alert raised. TN: benign, no alert. FN: real attack, no alert.
flashcards.back_example: An IDS stays silent while data is exfiltrated over DNS: false negative.
flashcards.back_confusion: False negatives are the most dangerous; false positives waste time and cause alert fatigue.
flashcards.back_hook: Positive = it alerted; true = it was right.

flashcards.back_definition: A network IDS watches traffic on a network segment. A host IDS watches one machine: its logs, files and processes.
flashcards.back_example: A HIDS notices a change to a system file that a NIDS cannot see inside encrypted traffic.
flashcards.back_confusion: Encryption limits what a NIDS can read, so host sensors fill the gap.
flashcards.back_hook: Watch the road vs watch the house.

flashcards.front: Full packet capture vs flow records?
flashcards.back_definition: Packet capture stores every packet with its contents: precise but costly. Flow records (NetFlow) summarise each conversation: who, ports, bytes, duration, with no payload.
flashcards.back_example: A flow record shows 4 GB sent to an unknown IP at 3 a.m.
flashcards.back_confusion: Most anomalies show up in flow data without reading any payload.
flashcards.back_hook: The full recording vs the phone bill.

flashcards.back_definition: A profile of normal traffic (volumes, ports, times, destinations) that current traffic is compared against.
flashcards.back_example: The finance server normally sends 200 MB a day; 9 GB today stands out.
flashcards.back_confusion: Baselines drift as the business changes, so they must be updated.
flashcards.back_hook: You can't spot strange until you know normal.

flashcards.back_definition: Regular, machine-timed outbound connections from malware checking in with its command-and-control server.
flashcards.back_example: A workstation contacts the same unknown IP every 15 minutes, all day and night.
flashcards.back_confusion: Some legitimate software also polls regularly, so check the destination and context.

flashcards.front: Which network signs point to data exfiltration?
flashcards.back_definition: A sudden spike in outbound data volume, transfers to unfamiliar destinations, odd hours, and unusual protocols such as very long DNS queries.
flashcards.back_example: 40 GB from a production server to an unknown IP between 2 and 3 a.m.
flashcards.back_confusion: An unusual port alone is a reason to investigate, not proof of compromise.
flashcards.back_hook: Too much, too far, too late at night.

flashcards.front: What does a SIEM do in network monitoring?
flashcards.back_definition: It collects logs and flow data from many sources, correlates them and alerts analysts, giving one place to search.
flashcards.back_example: Firewall, DNS and VPN logs together show one host's suspicious chain of events.
flashcards.back_confusion: A SIEM depends on the right logs being sent to it; missing sources are blind spots.

flashcards.front: Name the six incident response phases in order.
flashcards.back_definition: Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned (the SANS PICERL model). NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 groups the same steps into four phases.
flashcards.back_example: Writing the playbook is Preparation; isolating the infected host is Containment.
flashcards.back_confusion: Preparation happens before any incident; it is still a phase.
flashcards.back_hook: Please Investigate Carefully, Every Response Learns.

flashcards.back_definition: Removing malware before the threat is contained can tip off the attacker, who may switch to another foothold, and can lead to reinfection.
flashcards.back_example: Isolate the infected servers first, then remove the backdoor accounts.
flashcards.back_confusion: Containment stops the spread; eradication removes the cause.
flashcards.back_hook: Stop the bleeding, then remove the splinter.

flashcards.front: Why is Lessons Learned a required phase?
flashcards.back_definition: Recovery restores service, but without a review the weakness that allowed the incident usually stays.
flashcards.back_example: The review finds that MFA was missing on the VPN and fixes it everywhere.
flashcards.back_confusion: Back online is not the same as over.

flashcards.front: Why did Target miss its 2013 attackers despite alerts?
flashcards.back_definition: Its monitoring tools did raise alerts about the malware, but the team did not act on them in time: a gap between detection and response.
flashcards.back_example: Alerts were seen, judged low priority and not escalated.
flashcards.back_confusion: Buying detection tools is not the same as having a detection programme.
flashcards.back_hook: An alarm nobody answers is just noise.

flashcards.front: What made SolarWinds (2020) so hard to detect?
flashcards.back_definition: Attackers hid the SUNBURST backdoor inside a signed, legitimate Orion software update, so it arrived as trusted software and stayed quiet for weeks before contacting its servers.
flashcards.back_example: About 18,000 customers installed the poisoned update.
flashcards.back_confusion: Signature and reputation checks trusted it because it came from the real vendor.
flashcards.back_hook: The Trojan horse came with a receipt.
